An Anthropic mathematician indicates Claude helped him crack the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old puzzle with a $1 million prize attached.

His claim surfaced Friday, one day after the AI company’s stock-market debut, and has not yet been independently verified.

Sources indicate that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpöge wrote in a four-page note. He says the method also resolves the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which extends the question to other mathematical functions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Alpöge claims he and Claude encoded their argument in Lean, software used to check mathematical proofs step by step. His note links to 14 downloadable parts of the proof archive, but its availability does not amount to acceptance by the mathematical community.

In a recent development, alpöge says he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about a possible announcement “late Sunday night,” November 15. He then consulted manufacturer leadership and stated there was a constraint to respect, without explaining precisely what it was.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he acknowledged. Alpöge rejected a cynical interpretation of the timing, but did not explicitly say the company’s IPO caused the delay.

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday, November 19, after raising $81.34 billion in its offering.

Alpöge figured in September’s AI math wars. OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem as he and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster pursued related fluid-equation work, sparking a credit dispute over research priority.

OpenAI followed in October with 722 manuscripts generated by an unreleased model, grouped into 372 families of results. Only 162 included Lean-checked main results, and mathematicians demanded stronger evidence rather than accepting the organization’s flood of claims at face value.

Some mathematicians fear a “mathocalypse,” with AI solving coveted problems before researchers can learn from pursuing them. Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt warned that, without adaptation, “there’s just no more math in 50 years.” At an MIT panel this week, Buckmaster argued mathematics still requires human understanding.

It has been revealed that first posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

Recent findings suggest that lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Anthropic previously reported progress on the zeta function without claiming to solve the full hypothesis. Alpöge’s new assertion goes far beyond that earlier work.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Riemann hypothesis among its Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award. Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.

Tech Report: There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem.
  • It has been revealed that the class does not have a format in the traditional sense.
  • A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem. A pair of double doors swings lazily back and forth, marking a procession of students and the boxes they carry. DiGrazia leans against the wall, dressed in a red polo and khaki trousers, watching his small community unpack and ready itself for training.

It has been revealed that the class does not have a format in the traditional sense. There is no lantern-jawed instructor with a whistle and a clipboard. No snap of uniforms in sync with the rhythm of a kata. There is not even, as far as I could tell, a formal warm-up. Instead, the room seems to have its own sense of internal order.

A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs. Some—a breastplate, maybe a set of greaves—are singled out and ferried to a corner, where three individuals sit, cross-legged, and carefully hammer out the dents.

According to recent reports, ropes are thrown over the basketball hoops, and as soon as they land, students appear and begin practicing striking drills with blunted steel weapons. There are, admittedly, a lot of people with weapons. It’s a little surreal at first. When you encounter a fighter in full armor with a sword and buckler or a mace, there is a sense of visual cohesion. It is an entirely different matter to pass a fighter in cutoff denim and a T-shirt practicing elegant, sweeping strikes with an axe.

In a recent development, at the back of the room, the mats find their way into a rectangle, and small scrimmages begin with foam swords and shields. The training takes on its own rhythm; newer members train with foam swords and shields around the edges of the room, while the more seasoned fighters, now sporting what appear to be hockey helmets with face masks, begin grappling practice at its center. Everyone seems to know where they need to be and what they need to do.

It has been revealed that it’s taken a long time to get here—years, actually, 13 of them, to be precise. After serving in the military, DiGrazia traces a path through Columbia University, then Harvard, before landing a job at Morgan Stanley. Finding the rhythm of corporate life increasingly dull, he sought relief through extreme sports. DiGrazia started with the classics: marathons, ultramarathons, scuba diving, skydiving, martial arts. But nothing really stuck; he was always chasing something else. That is, until a happy accident. DiGrazia tried what he thought was going to be “full-contact” LARPing (live-action role-playing), but found the experience less than fulfilling: “You couldn't punch people, couldn't grapple people, couldn't kick people, nothing,” DiGrazia indicates. The participants were wearing plastic armor, and a hit to the leg saw fighters taking a theatrical knee and swiping at their opponents. At the end of the practice, however, DiGrazia found himself sticking around, commiserating with another fighter, Zorikh, whom he credits as starting his journey along a path that would lead to him founding Gladiators NYC, and laying the groundwork for The Armored League.

Recent findings suggest that modern armored combat has a longer history in Europe, and DiGrazia found himself bouncing all over the continent, fighting in Poland or next to a castle in Spain. If you wanted to fight in armor, Eastern Europe was where you had to go. Stateside, the early days were decidedly underground and homebrew. Your options were more limited: small groups of fighters met in parking lots and cornfields. Orlando Mendez, one of the founding members of Gladiators NYC, remembers “a lot of horse arenas.” They were one of the few places you could throw someone into a wall without complaint. It was a sport that grew anywhere it could find space. Jason Puerta, owner of Golden Ring Combat, a West Coast armored combat group, recalls regularly fighting on the lawns of a corporate campus after securing the bemused blessing of the local security outfit. It wasn’t quite Fight Club—newly introduced members were always welcome (and still are), and people were encouraged to talk about it. Instead, the group could be remarked to be self-selective: “You either got the hang of it, or you just turned in your armor at the end of the day,” DiGrazia recalls. There were few rules, no weight divisions, and no weapon classes.

In these early years, the attrition rate was high. DiGrazia estimates about half of the participants quit within weeks. Even when he first secured the community center and started spreading the word about classes, he remembers sitting on a bench in the gym, staring at the doors, waiting for someone, anyone, to come to a class. Eventually, they did.

In a recent development, the free classes, access to equipment, loaner armor, and the open exhibition matches in New York’s Central Park—all of these, he believes, must remain core elements of the community and the sport. Gladiators NYC also has a nonprofit arm called “Santa’s Knights” where armored knights go door to door during the holidays and deliver presents to children. His commitment to this approach has not come without difficulties. DiGrazia once partnered with a martial arts school whose owner forbade him from sponsoring students who could not afford the $30 class fee. That school closed during COVID.

Technically, the sport can trace its roots back to the 14th century, when knights, foot soldiers, and men-at-arms would practice combat using dull steel weapons and a mixture of soft and plate armor. It was a way to hone their skills in times of peace. The fundamentals of the practice remain in a number of combat sports to this day, but one need only watch a bout of Olympic fencing (or “pointy tag” as Mendez described it) to realize the distance traveled. The Armored League, however, doesn’t seek a return to its medieval origins or even to the stringently historically accurate expressions, which tend to dominate in Europe. When pressed about this, DiGrazia gives an exasperated sigh: “I don't want some librarian walking around looking with a fucking magnifying glass on everybody's goddamn rivet. Leave us alone. Let's have a good time.” The aim is to bring the spectacle and joy to fresh audiences.

Recent findings suggest that even if, at first, you cannot follow the scoring, the fights are pure melodrama. Like any combat sport, the fighters’ stats are declared as they enter the ring—with one key distinction: their weight includes their suit of armor. Short of a quirk, it communicates the impact of the sport in a more visceral way: when a pair of combatants crash to the ground or bounce off the chain-link fencing, that’s close to 600 pounds of flesh and steel set in ballistic motion.

Bouts are divided into three to five one-minute rounds. Points are awarded based on strikes—where they land and how hard. Basic, clean strikes with weapons, shields, or fists get a base number of points. Meanwhile headshots, two-handed weapon strikes, and slugging a downed opponent get you even more. The bouts are judged by a panel set to one side of the ring, while a pair of counters runs frantically around the perimeter counting strikes.

It has been revealed that there are comparatively few rules beyond some basic safety precautions: no stabbing or thrusting; no stomping; no strikes at the inner elbows, armpits, or the backs of knees; no slashing at the neck; and no submissions. Save for these, anything goes, and this adds to the thrill of the fights. Fighters are also not limited to their weapons, and in some cases, they will stand and trade blows like boxers. Though all of the serious fighters have broad and varied martial arts backgrounds—and training approaches—there's a roughly consistent path that leads to The Armored League. Snatches of Muay Thai knee strikes, judo sweeps, classical boxing, escrima, and BJJ are all visible in the blur of limbs, steel, and weapons. One can only imagine how the “librarians” would feel about that.

Strikes may come in flurries or great arcs, but most are hard enough to send sparks flying off the helmets. There is a marshal in the ring with the fighters, notably unarmored save for a yellow flag that’s mainly used to break the fighters up at the end of each round, which frequently ends in a tangle of armor and weapons on the floor of the ring.

Industry observers note that there are two elements that, despite the passage of centuries, have not changed: cost and danger. Historians are divided on the exact conversion rate between 1400 and today, and most put it in terms of wages. They quote the cost of a full set of armor at somewhere between 12 and 18 months of pay. What’s universally agreed upon is that arms and armor were (and remain) anything but cheap. A full suit—then, as now—weighs anywhere from 60 to 80 pounds.

Recent findings suggest that this century, prices start at around $5,000 and climb precipitously with customization. It can take anywhere from a few weeks to a year for delivery. Most participants build their suits over time as they are drawn deeper into the sport.

Sources indicate that building a full set is not easy. A cursory search online will lead you to a number of pages, which might appear to offer armor, but these sites are largely focused on cosplayers or LARPers. That armor will certainly hold together for a walk through Comic-Con, but it will do little to protect from a real blow. The handful of armorers still working today have long wait lists. Puerta notes that despite this, the communal nature of the sport means that much of the armor is passed down or traded between the combatants: as someone upgrades or hangs up their helmet, the armor finds its way into a new pair of hands or onto a new person’s shoulders. At Gladiators NYC, fighters who graduate from the classes, from “softs” (padded armor), and wish to try their hand at the real thing, can borrow pieces from Gladiators NYC’s own armory.

Sources indicate that amongst the current fighters who regularly participate in Armored League matches, almost all fight in custom armor. The suits must adhere to certain safety standards—thickness of steel, comprehensive eye protection, etc. But beyond that, there’s ample room for self-expression.

For example, Abeid “Mando” Mitchell fights in comparatively minimalist and lightweight armor and is readily recognizable by his distinctive helmet, which was made in the style of the Mandalorian from Star Wars. Luke “The Red Knight of Brooklyn” has assembled what he refers to as “a sporting replica” of 1480s armor in keeping with his own, more classical concerns.

Despite the care and attention each fighter devotes to their own armor, at all of the matches I attended, I saw weapons traded freely, shields swapped, even gauntlets lent. For as much violence as there is inside of a 60-second round, there is an equal, if not greater, level of care at the bell. The armor is not just for show; it’s for safety. Combatants want to win as much as they want to ensure their opponent walks off the field under their own power. It’s a fine balance, and as Mendez put it, “once you put on the armor and you get your ass beat a couple of times,” everybody is basically friends.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, it takes a toll. Puerta told me a story of how he almost lost his left eye when the tip of a sword slipped through the bars of his helmet. Others relayed stories of being crushed in a melee and of “helmet terrors” where breathing heavily in the confines of a helmet causes a buildup of carbon dioxide and creates a sensation similar to drowning.

In a recent development, what does the future look like? In my time with the League and Gladiators NYC, I sensed I was watching a sport in its adolescence. It is a league and community that seems to blink in the stark light of its own success and rapidly growing audience. Social media has made it easier for these once disparate communities to connect; the cornfields and horse rinks have been parlayed into an Octagon at the Melrose Ballroom in Queens or a showcase at a theater in Times Square. The bleachers that once held a smattering of friends and family have shifted into crowds drawn from all walks of life—at the sold-out show in Queens, the lines stretched around the block and some people waited an hour just to get into the venue. The Central Park exhibition matches, which happen every second Saturday of the month, have begun to draw crowds that can number over a thousand.

DiGrazia and his merry band have come a long way from the leaner years, when they struggled to find space to practice, the years when they fought in the parking lots of regional hotels in the Midwest or in the summer heat on the boardwalk in Coney Island.

Industry observers note that still, there is, for now, little to no money in this sport. The community, and the fighters too, all have day jobs. They are PhD students, fitness instructors, photographers, and graphic designers. One manages a magic and costume shop. Again, Fight Club springs to mind, as each goes about their day job, bearing the marks of a Thursday brawl or a weekend match, one can only wonder if anyone sees a bruise sticking out of a shirt sleeve and stops to ask just where it came from.

Kia isn’t wasting any time updating its Sportage-sized EV5 electric SUV. Leaked images just gave us our first look at what’s changing.

While Kia doesn’t sell the EV5 in the US, the electric SUV has been a hit in other global markets. It first went on sale in China in 2023, and Kia rolled out the global model last year; it is now available in Europe, Canada, the UK, and other overseas regions.

The electric SUV has played a major part in Kia’s turnaround in China and is among the top-selling EVs in places like Australia.

Kia is already preparing to introduce an updated version in 2027. The updated EV5 was revealed through Australian Design Rule (ADR) regulatory documents, including images of the latest version and some powertrain specs.

Front- and all-wheel-drive variants will get a power boost with up to 234 hp (175 kW) in FWD and 334 hp (249 kW) for AWD models.

The latest EV5 will still use the same 64.2 kWh and 88.1 kWh battery packs, but updated range figures have yet to be unveiled.

Kia’s current model offers a WLTP range of up to 248 miles (400 km) from the smaller battery and 345 miles (555 km) from the larger battery.

As previous spy images have shown, the updated Kia EV5 features a few slight exterior design changes.

These changes include newly introduced front and rear bumpers, similar to those of the rugged EV5 WKNDR Concept Kia revealed last November at the Guangzhou Motor Show.

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car).

Saying there are updates with no context is borderline useless. A power boost from what? The EV5 isn't in the US, so I don't have its looks anywhere close to memorized.

Hopefully the power increase is more than just a software patch, having hardware updates for better efficiency/lower weight/lower costs even if they're not passed on to consumers. If they're updating the looks, they should coincide with better aerodynamics for better higher speed range and efficiency.

Recent spy photos in Korea from ShortsCar revealed the EV5 upgrade features a 27″ center infotainment screen, similar to the Hyundai Elexio and Kia Seltos that are made in China.

A sticker on the back noted the vehicle was destined for the Philippines, meaning it’s the EV5 that’s produced in China.

Since Kia launched the China-made EV5 in 2023, it’s due for a refresh around 2027. Whether and when Kia will introduce the updated global version, which is produced in Korea, has yet to be confirmed.

#52780. Latest Update: 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

Latest Update: 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor.
  • We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” notes global editorial director Amy Astley. “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!”.

We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD-approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present.

Recent findings suggest that there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home. Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley says in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors.

It has been revealed that created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work.

Industry observers note that global features director Sam Cochran’s debut coffee table book opens with the words, “Nothing is interesting unless it is personal.” His project, American Designers at Home, brings that idea to life beautifully. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—says, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur.

It has been revealed that levasseur states that Simon Upton’s most recent release with Rizzoli contains “beauty and poetry on every page.” The title is a nod to the iconic London A–Z: The detailed street atlas that every Londoner seemed to own in the 1980s and early 2000s, pre-Google Maps. Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.”.

In a recent development, this beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” claims senior digital editor Catherine Hong. “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration.".

In a recent development, “Whether or not you’d ever dare to decorate with Sasha Bikoff’s over-the-top flair, this book is guaranteed to make a splash on your coffee table,” notes Hong. Behind its trippy, hot-pink cover lies screaming color, clashing eras, and utter fantasy. The designer lives by her “Rule of Three Wows”—chronicled in the pages—and her book is, accordingly, loud, wildly fun, and a little bit insane in the best way.

Recent findings suggest that studio Valle de Valle’s debut monograph offers a refined window into the AD100 firm’s singular vision and creative evolution—surveying 10 projects from the past 10 years. Printed in Italy, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson, the pages demonstrate the firm’s interior philosophy of creating spaces that feel personal, layered, and deeply inhabitable. “The edition isn’t just a tour de visual force, it’s an art object unto itself,” claims Cochran. “I would expect nothing less from these brilliant auteurs.".

Sources indicate that “One of Meyer Davis’s greatest strengths is how cofounders Will Meyer and Gray Davis distill references, ideas, and desires into a highly refined vision,” notes AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach. As client Jenna Lyons puts it in the book’s foreword, “They gave me clarity.” Beyond a printed body of work, The Language of Home is a testament to the collaborations that shape the studio's warm, reductive interiors. Designed with honest materials and a contemporary lens, the featured residences—a modern glass house in the Berkshires and an earthen dwelling in Puerto Escondido—reflect their inhabitants with a calm, clear ease.

Recent findings suggest that the inaugural monograph from AD100 design duo Humbert & Poyet showcases their signature brand of eclectic French luxury, blending Art Deco glamour, midcentury modernism, and the decorative arts. Spanning residential and hospitality projects around the world, the book by AD contributing editor Gay Gassmann takes readers from a French Riviera villa to a Milan restaurant housed in a 17th-century chapel, with stops in Upcoming York, Paris, Monaco, and Seoul.

In New York: Atelier AM, Alexandra and Michael Misczynkski, the married couple behind the AD100 firm, shine a light on their New York projects, all beautifully captured by François Halard. Spotlighting a range of projects like elegant Manhattan residences and more relaxed Long Island retreats, contributor Ingrid Abramovitch states the book itself is “equally exquisite, with a cover resembling wood grain, and high-gloss pages printed in Italy.”.

Industry observers note that 2026 AD New American Voices honoree Amber Guyton first burst onto the design scene by way of her hit blog, Blessed Little Bungalow. “Her debut book brings the same wit and spirit to the printed page in a kaleidoscope of color and pattern,” says Cochran. Senior shopping editor Nashia Baker adds that the pages “truly embody how to bring personality to any room.” Throughout the book, she makes a case for maximalism, and distills her approach into four pillars: joy, culture, layers, and intention.

Industry observers note that “This book is perfect for cinephiles, design-lovers, or anyone with a case of wanderlust,” claims senior digital editor Rachel Wallace. Film is one way to travel the world without ever leaving the sofa, and with her upcoming project On Location, longtime AD contributor Cathy Whitlock takes readers on a global cinematic journey. The book goes behind the scenes of films that make you want to hop on a flight and never look back. Colorful Mexico City scenes from Frida and Marie Antoinette’s famous Palace of Versailles shooting location are both represented.

Organized by a series of chapter essays rather than specific projects, AD100 designer Dan Fink’s debut book explores bigger questions on how spaces, objects, and compositions move us across time. At the same time, the book spotlights several career-defining projects from his namesake studio, including previously unpublished interiors like Manhattan penthouses, Hawaiian beach retreats, Hollywood homes, and more.

One of the few completely fail-proof gifts is one of the best coffee table books of the season—weighty tomes whose thick, glossy pages feature stunning photographs and illustrations, to be specific. On a superficial level, they add ambiance, whether you place them in a library or a living room. But the best ones live in your home forever, while expanding your horizons far beyond. They also come across as far more memorable and thoughtful than the expected candle or bottle of champagne. Like works of fiction, there are limitless topics that can make deciding on an eye-catching hardcover (that doubles as home decor) seemingly impossible.

But that’s where we come in. Our team has gathered its favorite giftable recommendations for everyone from tennis enthusiasts to globe-trotters to interior design aficionados. From a book focused on hotels around the world to another that spotlights Tokyo style, there are plenty of ways to adorn the coffee tables of all the people on your holiday gift list. Most of them came out in 2024, but we’ve also included a few evergreen picks that make worthy gifts any year.

Plus, if you’re down to the wire on last-minute gifts, rest assured that most of these selections are available (and even marked down ahead of the holidays!) on Amazon.

Après-ski style needs no introduction in a season full of fuzzy Fair Isle sweaters, but it’s the cozy interiors of the chalets along the world’s most popular ski slopes that are worthy of a second look. From the wooden beams of an A-frame to the blazing fireplaces set within them, AD contributor Kathryn O’Shea-Evans pores over the finer details in this fun, wintery escape.

As associate digital editor Maya Ibbitson previously described it, “Alpine Style is a true compendium of resort luxury,” spanning spectacular chalets from Gstaad to Aspen and featuring the works of AD PRO Directory members such as Massucco Warner, Robbins Architecture, and Kara Adam Interiors.

Japan’s interiors are a perpetual reference for modern-day designers, and whether you’re a proponent of wabi-sabi principles or just looking for small space ideas, Tokyo Style will help you explore both.

Originally published in 1993, it’s since become a collector’s item and cult classic, and it was recommended by commerce writer Julia Harrison for anyone who would appreciate a more intimate glimpse of Tokyo’s dwellings: “Apartamento, an imprint that consistently delivers on elite design, has reintroduced Tsuzuki’s collection for us to enjoy in its full brilliance—that is, not a ‘fine’ condition original at $170 with $90 shipping from eBay.”.

It has been revealed that prefaced with a foreword by Spike Lee, BLK MKT Vintage peers into the world of the Brooklyn antique shop’s endlessly curious founders Jannah Handy and Kiyanna Stewart. “This monograph teems with more than 300 studies of vintage ephemera and reads like a collage with context, or an I spy for your inner adult archivist,” writes Ibbitson of the book. For collectors, Sydney Gore pinpoints it as a must-have for your rotation.

Donald Judd’s considered, minimalist approach to design has fostered its own cult of acolytes who, these days, emulate his daybeds and chairs on Instagram.

Sources indicate that for the true Juddheads, the Judd Foundation has produced a new book edited by his children Rainer and Flavin Judd that chronicles more than one hundred of his functional works produced between 1970 and 1992. “Mixed in are the juiciest bits: photos from past and present of those pieces in Judd-designed spaces in New York and Marfa,” Ibbitson writes.

AD’s Milan correspondent Laura May Todd penned a delightful homage to Italian living this year, one which spans from historic palaces in Venice to the homes of creatives like Luca Guadagnino along with midcentury Milanese apartments, so you can enjoy a small taste of la dolce vita on each page.

It was one of the AD PRO team’s favorite book releases this fall, one which should suit the person on your list who never got over their Italian study abroad or is manifesting a Sicilian villa in their future.

For the person on your list who delights in having people over, How They Entertain, released this fall, serves as a comprehensive guide to (and celebration of) the art of hosting.

Written by Pierre Sauvage, it’s chock-full of inspiration for your next dinner party, from recipes to design notes on arranging a tabletop to remember, as well as interviews with tastemakers like Laura Gonzalez about their particular philosophy on entertaining guests.

Considering this year’s smash summer hit Challengers and the enduring popularity of tenniscore (polos, skorts, and all), it’s clear that tennis is a lifestyle that has captured the imagination of many people, avid tennis players or not.

This book recommended by the AD PRO team earlier this year is dedicated to a more, uh, underserved cross section of the sport: the backdrops where athletes volley their way to tournament glory (clay, grass, asphalt, and beyond) in locales from Queens to Kenya.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent is no stranger to the pages of this very magazine, and his new book is a friends and family affair studded with stars, like Oprah and legendary choreographer Fatima Robinson, with whom Brent has formed close connections over the past 20 years.

We’ve previously described the book (layered with sentimental photos and fresh snapshots of contributors in their home) as “more scrapbook than design manifesto, a love letter to the spaces that people have inhabited and inherited over the years.” Read AD’s extensive interview with Brent for more backstory behind (and tidbits from) the book.

It has been revealed that for art buffs with a fondness for the Harlem Renaissance—an era synonymous with greats like Aaron Douglas, known as the father of African-American art—this new book compiled by MoMA curator Denise Murrell is an excellent title to know. “Having this book is about as close as you’ll ever get to owning one of the original masterpieces featured in the Harlem Renaissance exhibition at The Met,” Gore claims.

Sources indicate that self-interested plug here, but we really couldn’t publish a guide to coffee table books without mentioning our own, AD at 100: A Century of Style. For the design buff with an appetite for lush interiors and a healthy curiosity for how A-listers live, there’s no more satisfying holiday treat than this tome that delves into the homes of the Obamas, David Hockney, Diana Vreeland, and beyond. It also serves as a bird’s eye view of a century in design and architecture, including the works of Frank Gehry, David Hicks, Frank Lloyd Wright, and much, much more.

Architecture has a reputation for myopia when it comes to its foremost voices, but this book seeks to rectify the past with a fresh overview of some of its most brilliant underrepresented talents, including interviews with female architects around the globe such as Tatiana Bilbao, Liz Diller, and Julia Gamolina.

“100 Women offers a refreshing reframe of the built environment outside of the male-dominated Western canon, proving the benefits of sourcing alternative points of reference,” Ibbitson wrote of it in AD PRO’s guide to the best latest design books out this past spring.

Colony founder Jean Lin has mentored and platformed some of the design world’s brightest rising stars, and in her first book out this year, she tapped a wide pool of creatives to explore the concept of collections that inform their work, from ceramicist Stephanie H. Shih’s cache of soy sauce bottles to Mira Nakashima’s stockpile of lumber inherited from her father, architect turned furniture maker George Nakashima.

That’s just one facet of the book Ibbitson previously described as an “encyclopedic, elemental study of artist studios, profiles, materials, and everything else under the design umbrella,” with plenty of wisdom imparted within its pages, from how-tos to styling tips. Read our interview with Lin for more of her notes on curating a collection of your own.

Luna Luna—a 1980s artist-led amusement park featuring works by icons of the art world such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Salvador Dalí, and David Hockney—is experiencing a resurgence as of late, what with a new retrospective at The Shed this year, along with a revival of the park itself in Los Angeles late last year.

Sources indicate that this 2023 book takes a deeper dive into Luna Luna’s history blending fine art with the playful energy of a carnival—encompassing rides, interactive installations, and surreal sculptures. It comes recommended by associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz, who nods to the book’s breadth of archival media within, from photos to sketches, that are accompanied by behind-the-scenes stories.

For jet-setters who love to live large on vacation, Spencer Bailey’s Design: The Leading Hotels of the World (released just this month) is one sure way to sustain a sense of wanderlust. His upcoming book takes readers on a visual journey to 80 countries around the globe, inviting them to mentally book into sumptuous spaces from The Okura in Tokyo to the Portrait Hotel in Milan. It’s rounded out by notable travel and design writers like Maria Cristina Didero and Mark Ellwood, who lend us their travel tips, on top of their reflections on the lodgings featured within.

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, I’ve been known to have questionable standards in some areas of life—like my preference for boxed wine post-grad or my ability to convince myself that cereal counts as dinner. But when it comes to what I put on my feet, the bar is high. I used to think a good walking shoe just meant something that didn’t give me blisters. Now, as a style writer with a pile of sneakers so high it rivals Everest, I expect a lot more. I’m talking support, tons of comfort, and yes, style. That’s exactly why Brooks has become my go-to. The brand’s secret sauce: a perfectly balanced, firm-yet-plush cushioning that makes long days on my feet feel like a walk in the park.

Brooks has been around for over 100 years, and the brand has perfected its walking (and running) shoes. It’s no wonder that Brooks sneakers also come highly recommended by our team of active editors and podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM. “Brooks has always been one of my go-to shoes, especially for walking,” notes Schaeffer. That’s thanks to their ideal balance of comfort and support, extensive sizing, secure laces, and breathable, sturdy mesh uppers. You need a shoe specifically for walking because it offers the necessary cushion to take the impact off your joints and give your foot the support it needs to propel forward. These features help prevent aches and injuries.

According to recent reports, there’s a seemingly endless amount of sneakers to choose from, but don’t stress: I’ve put in the work to try out the best Brooks shoes for walking. I log (at least) 10,000 steps per day between walking my energetic Jack Russell terrier all around Long Island and commuting into Manhattan for work. Our team of editors also tested every Brooks sneaker through power walking, long days at the office, and leisurely strolls. Our favorite shoe of the bunch is the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, but many others came close for their cushion and stability.

It has been revealed that after testing dozens of shoes, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26 takes the crown as my go-to for walking (and tbh, everything else). The latest Adrenaline GTS iteration still nails the balance between cushion and support, keeping my stride steady without feeling stiff or squished—which is exactly what I loved about the 25.

According to recent reports, what really seals the deal? The firm-yet-cozy midsole hugs the foot just right, offering a secure, locked-in feel that still stays comfortable mile after mile. The 26 has about the same amount of cushioning as the previous version (maybeee a tinge more). It’s the perfect amount of cushion to keep feet comfy without sacrificing stability. The mesh upper got an upgrade too, with even more perforations to keep things cool even on the hottest days. I also love that Brooks kept the 10mm heel-to-toe drop (as opposed to the GTS 24's 12mm drop), which helps reduce the potential for strain in the hips and knees. I just snagged the 26 two weeks ago, but so far, I’ve racked up 15+ walking miles and 5 running miles, pain-free.

It has been revealed that the previous Adrenaline iteration actually took home the top spot for walking shoes in our 2026 Fitness Awards for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. And so far, the Adrenaline GTS 26 is looking like a superb contender, keeping all of our favorite details of its younger sibling while improving breathability.

My favorite thing about both versions is the shoe’s GuideRails tech, which uses firm foam on either side of the heel to keep feet locked in. The foam is infused with nitrogen, making it super comfortable and lightweight without being overly plush. Bonus: The (did I mention breathable?) mesh upper keeps things comfy without too much stretch (key for stability while walking), Schaeffer states.

Sources indicate that one heads-up: the Adrenaline GTS 26 is one of the heavier shoes on this list at 9.6 oz., so if you like a super lightweight shoe, you may want to consider the Glycerin Flex. However, I actually find this sneaker feels way lighter thanks to the mesh upper.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Industry observers note that if versatility is your priority, the Brooks Ghost 18 delivers. With its nitrogen-fused cushioning, the latest version of the shoe packs in the same amount of plush padding that we loved in the Ghost 17 (it was a 2025 WH Sneaker Award winner for a reason!). Impressively, the moderately high stack height at the heel doesn’t feel too squishy or wobbly. It’s a great do-it-all shoe for long walks, standing all day, and running.

Recent findings suggest that upgrades from the previous version include a newly introduced sockliner that makes for a comfy, snug fit and a flat tongue (the old one was a more classic padded option). “It does a good job of hugging the shape of your ankle without rubbing or chafing,” notes fitness writer and WH contributor Korin Miller. “I like the smooth, seamless feel it creates, but I noticed that the edges start to curl in with repeated use.” I’ve noticed the same, but it’s definitely not an problem once your foot is in the shoe—just something to double-check when you slide your foot in.

I’ve worn these for long walks with my pup, all-day errands, a Costco shopping spree (IYKYK), and a full day on my feet at a music festival—and my arches stayed happy through it all. The soft midsole offers that just-right level of give that absorbs impact without feeling too soft or marshmallowy. The knit mesh upper is even more breathable than in the last version, adding to the barely-there feel, as does the plush ankle collar, which doesn’t chafe or rub at all.

It has been revealed that one of my only gripes about the Ghost 17 was the slightly narrow toe box, but thankfully, the Ghost 18 solved this problem for me. It’s much more spacious now, both in terms of width and height.

Read More: Brooks Ghost 18 Review.

If you’re after a walking shoe that’s super cushy, the Brooks Glycerin 23 is it. I’ve tested these on nearly 10-mile walks through nature preserves and standing for hours at the DMV (ugh). I never once felt like my feet were sore or that I needed to rush to sit down—these things felt like walking on pillows.

Industry observers note that but the cushioning isn’t the only win here. The Glycerin 23’s knit upper gives this shoe a sock-like feel that hugs your foot without squeezing. It’s smooth, stretchy, and breathable, making it one of the most comfortable shoes I’ve worn on long walks. The shoe has a mild heel drop that helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot and reduces foot fatigue, which I sometimes experience with other walking shoes. While I wouldn’t quite describe the shoe as sleek or minimalist, it balances its plush cushioning with a more understated silhouette (aka it doesn’t veer into chunky dad shoe territory).

Industry observers note that I also appreciate how well this shoe performs on uneven surfaces thanks to its wide platform and ample traction. The durable outsole covers plenty of ground, and the traction has a complex, winding tread pattern. I never feel like I’m going to slip, even on slick pavement.

Industry observers note that so far, the Glycerin 23 does a great job of keeping my feet locked in despite its super thick cushioning—but it’s not designed for max stability. Those with specific foot problems, like plantar fasciitis or issues with overpronation, may want to pick a slightly less cushioned, more supportive shoe, like the Adrenaline GTS 25.

Read More: The Best Shoes For Standing All Day.

According to recent reports, the Brooks Ghost Max 3 took home the top spot in our guide to the most comfortable sneakers for its perfect balance of maximum support and cushioning. It keeps my feet comfortably locked in, even after hours of wear, and my ankles never feel wobbly, which often happens with plush shoes like this one.

“Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!),” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. I agree. That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it almost feels like walking on a moving runway at the airport.

Even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s super stable thanks to its signature Guardrails tech (the same found in the Adrenaline GTS 25). The outsole also has a broad base, which reduces rolling of the foot inward and outward and cradles the foot in place without interfering with your stride. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says these features are great for high arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel one ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options.

Sources indicate that during testing, we did notice some wear and tear on the upper pretty early on (after a few months). While it was a bit of a bummer, the elite combo of cushion and support keeps this kick high on my list of Brooks sneakers.

Read more: Best Walking Shoes for Women.

Think of the Glyceric Flex as Glycerin 23’s lighter, more flexible counterpart. The upper and outsole are both made from super bendy materials that give the shoe an almost barefoot feel.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a big fan of this shoe for walking, long periods of standing, running, and plyometric workouts. It's incredibly versatile, thanks to ample nitrogen-infused cushioning and a flexible midsole. The FlexZone technology—a strategically placed groove in the center of the shoe’s outsole—helps enhance the shoe’s flexibility and allows the foot to move naturally. Combined with the pods under the front of the foot (which reminds me of On’s signature CloudTec system you see on most of the brand’s outsoles), the shoe has a super bouncy feel without feeling wobbly.

It has been revealed that bonus: at only 8.0 ounces, it's the lightest shoe on this list, so your feet won’t feel bogged down. But it still falls in Schaeffer’s recommended weight range (eight to 10 ounces), so it's hefty enough to keep your foot locked in. Plus, the flat knit upper is super soft, breathable, and—yes—flexible, which adds to its airy feel.

But the shoe’s lighter weight means it offers less heft and a less supportive feel. If you need more structure or have specific stability needs, these might not be your best bet. But, if you’re into a flexible, responsive shoe that doesn’t weigh you down—this one’s tough to beat.

The Brooks Ghost Max L offers a super plush, easygoing stride. The high-stacked cushioning is next-level—soft but stable, like walking on a marshmallow. It has an outsole with a curved bottom, like a rocking chair, to help propel you forward so each step takes a bit less energy.

Industry observers note that I didn’t expect to notice the rocker bottom that much, but I totally get the hype. Schaeffer says he actually prefers rocker-bottom shoes for walking, especially as we get older, because they help take pressure off joints. That mentioned, the same rocker technology makes me feel a little off-balance when I try to run or power walk in them, so I keep these strictly for leisurely walks and casual wear.

Looks-wise, I’m team Ghost Max L all the way. Some might say the stacked foam gives grandma shoes, but I think it strikes that perfect balance of chunky and cool—especially when styled right. I like to wear mine with a wide-leg pant and a blazer on top. It’s got just the right amount of bulk to feel trendy without being clunky, and pairs well with everything from athleisure to workwear.

However, this shoe runs small. Definitely size up if you’re in between sizes or like a little wiggle room. I could have used a half size larger than what I wear in the rest of my Brooks shoes for a little more comfort, but I still get a lot of casual wear out of them regardless.

Recent findings suggest that first things first, you want a good mix of comfort and stability in your walking shoe, notes Schaeffer. He recommends looking for a pair that cups your heel in a way that isn’t too snug or too loose. This feature will keep your feet from wobbling with every step you take. That sort of stability keeps your foot aligned as you walk, which is key for overpronation (foot rolls in too much) or underpronation (foot rolls out), helping prevent strain on your joints and maintaining balance. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but Shaeffer says to avoid any that are overly cushioned, and instead look for a shoe that is a bit sturdier to keep your feet in neutral alignment to avoid foot fatigue and prevent sprains or strains.

Sources indicate that the front of your sneaker (aka toe box) should never be too snug because it can pinch the nerves and inflame the ball of your foot (aka metatarsalgia). One way to know if your toe box is wide enough? Make sure your foot lies one thumb width from the side of the shoe and one thumb width from the front of the shoe. Tip: If you have a longer second toe, a larger toe box is even more key, Schaeffer indicates.

Brooks is famous for its incredible arch support, which is exactly what Schaeffer states to look for in a walking shoe. However, if your arches need a little extra TLC, Schaeffer suggests getting insoles that cater to your specific foot needs. He recommends Dr. Scholl’s Multipurpose Insoles or custom orthotics. "The insoles help with alignment and keep you balanced," he says, which is especially vital if you suffer from chronic pain, plantar fasciitis, or concerns with your feet rolling inward or outward while you walk. If this sounds like you, we def recommend scheduling a visit with a podiatrist to make sure your feet get the care they need.

It has been revealed that A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer notes to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Schaeffer says most people love a lightweight shoe since it's nice to feel like there's nothing down there. Just make sure the shoe has a supportive feel, and it holds your foot with every step you take. "In this case, I'm okay with the shoe being light," he says. "But, if the shoe is too light (under four ounces), you sacrifice function and stability." All of the Brooks sneakers on this list are between eight and 10 ounces, so they're the perfect weight in Schaeffer's book.

In a recent development, over the past two years, the Women’s Health team has undertaken a comprehensive approach to curating the ultimate guide to the best Brooks walking shoes by testing nearly every new pair as it drops. Along with insights from Brad Schaeffer, DPM, board-certified foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City, we’ve put more than 30 Brooks sneakers through their paces.

It has been revealed that as the associate style and reviews editor, I led the testing process with support from fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, and fitness and reviews editor Charles Thorp, NASM. Our evaluation involved multiple phases, consulting runners and walkers on the Women's Health team, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We subjected each shoe to everything from fast walks to long travel days to leisurely strolls. The narrowed-down list above includes the six shoes we were most impressed by.

Navigating the Unpredictable Ride of COPD

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HOOVES THUNDER AGAINST packed dirt as the bull bucks to the left and the rider leans right, tightening his grip on the rope.
  • The unexpected twists and turns of a bull ride may feel familiar to people living with inadequately controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
  • Mark H., 60, has experienced the challenges that can come with COPD since he was diagnosed in 2010.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sponsored by Sanofi and Regeneron.

HOOVES THUNDER AGAINST packed dirt as the bull bucks to the left and the rider leans right, tightening his grip on the rope. Just as he finds his balance, another sudden buck or turn can change the course of the ride.

The unexpected twists and turns of a bull ride may feel familiar to people living with inadequately controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Not knowing when breathing challenges or a flare-up—a period when breathing becomes more difficult than usual that can last for several days—might occur can make everyday life feel unpredictable.

Mark H., 60, has experienced the challenges that can come with COPD since he was diagnosed in 2010. “COPD isn’t easy to navigate, and it can be a frightening condition to face,” he indicates. “I tried to ignore my diagnosis early on because I didn’t want to believe it, and I didn’t want to think about how it might affect my life. But ignoring it didn’t stop my COPD from making itself known. Shortness of breath was really impacting my day to day.”.

With support and clinical intervention, Mark was able to better manage his COPD and get back to doing more of the things he loves. Now, he wants others living with COPD to know help is available to manage their condition.

COPD IS A complex and progressive disease that can make breathing more difficult over time.

COPD can be caused by inflammation in the airways that causes damage to parts of your lungs. Patients with COPD may also have chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema.

Industry observers note that people with COPD can experience persistent cough, excessive mucus production, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Understanding COPD is important, and recognizing when the disease may not be adequately controlled is critical. Living with uncertainty around flare-ups can carry an emotional weight as well, says Corinne Young, nurse practitioner, pulmonary disease specialist, who is the Founder/Executive Director of the Association of Pulmonary Advanced Practice Providers.

Flare-ups, also known as exacerbations, are the worsening of COPD symptoms over several days. They can happen to anyone with COPD. During a flare-up, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and coughing can intensify and take longer to resolve. Even one flare-up can lead to permanent lung damage.

Young, who in addition to seeing patients, competes in team roping at rodeos, knows the importance of paying attention to changing conditions—a perspective she brings to helping patients recognize when their COPD may be inadequately controlled.

“The biggest predictor of a flare-up is a previous flare-up, and they start to get closer and closer together,” Young explains. For example, someone may experience a flare-up or exacerbation once every two years, then once a year, then every six months, then every three. “Inflammatory responses in the body drive these exacerbations, and that may lower lung function,” Young adds. That decline can increase the risk of additional flare-ups, perpetuating the cycle.

AS MARK’S COPD became more difficult to manage, it increasingly interfered with the life he was used to living. Shortness of breath and frequent flare-ups made it harder to work, travel, and do as many of the things he enjoyed. Eventually, he made the difficult decision to retire early from his job as a field service engineer.

Sources indicate that even after stepping away from work, Mark continued to struggle with his COPD. “I remember feeling like, ‘Well, I guess this is my life now,’” he says.

IN THE FALL of 2024, Mark underwent a pulmonary function test, bracing for bad news. The results confirmed that his current treatment proposal was no longer adequately managing his COPD, prompting a discussion with his pulmonologist about what to do next. His doctor explained that Mark’s high eosinophil count could be a sign of type 2 inflammation. With this information, Mark and his doctor explored other treatment options, including Dupixent® (dupilumab).

It has been revealed that dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Dupixent is not used to relieve sudden breathing problems and will not replace an inhaled rescue medicine.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in Dupixent.

Dupixent can cause serious side effects, such as allergic reactions, including skin reactions, that can sometimes be severe, eye problems, and joint aches and pain.

Please see additional Important Safety Information below.

Recent findings suggest that mark noticed a difference after adding Dupixent. “I could breathe better,” he notes. Now, Mark feels less winded, and he’s doing more of the things he loves. “I’m really grateful that I can enjoy my hobbies more without constantly thinking about my COPD,” he adds.

For Mark, better breathing started with an honest conversation. Young encourages anyone living with COPD to be open with their healthcare provider, who can explain the full range of treatment options available. “It’s not just inhalers anymore—there are a lot of options,” she indicates.

Like bull riders who stay alert to changing conditions, people living with COPD can watch for signs that their disease may be inadequately controlled and talk with their doctor about their treatment options. With the right support, they may be able to enjoy more of the moments that matter to them—including, for some, time spent in the rodeo stands.

IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION & INDICATION.

Dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in DUPIXENT®.

Before using DUPIXENT, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions, including if you:.

Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements.

According to recent reports, especially tell your healthcare provider if you are taking oral, topical, or inhaled corticosteroid medicines or have COPD and also have asthma. Do not change or stop your other medicines, including corticosteroid medicine or other asthma medicine, without talking to your healthcare provider. This may cause other symptoms that were controlled by those medicines to come back.

DUPIXENT can cause serious side effects, including:.

The most common side effects in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease include injection site reactions, common cold symptoms (nasopharyngitis), high count of a certain white blood cell (eosinophilia), viral infection, back pain, inflammation inside the nose (rhinitis), diarrhea, stomach problems (gastritis), joint pain (arthralgia), toothache, headache, and urinary tract infection.

Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effect that bothers you or that does not go away. These are not all the possible side effects of DUPIXENT. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch, or call 1-800-FDA-1088.

Use DUPIXENT exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. It’s an injection given under the skin (subcutaneous injection). Your healthcare provider will decide if you or your caregiver can inject DUPIXENT. Do not try to prepare and inject DUPIXENT until you or your caregiver have been trained by your healthcare provider.

Please see accompanying full Prescribing Information including Patient Information.

Learn more about Dupixent at Dupixent.com/COPD.

DUPIXENT is a registered trademark of Sanofi or an affiliate.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Texas-based startup (and resurrector of an old name) REO Trucks unveiled its revamped and renewed mission and previewed its first vehicle this past summer, but as of Monday, the American startup has some trucks to show us.
  • All three vehicles REO intends to release are detailed and pictured here.
  • The T4X will be the first to go on sale (targeting late 2028) according to the brand, and it has a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Texas-based startup (and resurrector of an old name) REO Trucks unveiled its revamped and renewed mission and previewed its first vehicle this past summer, but as of Monday, the American startup has some trucks to show us. Or, at least some renderings of some vehicles, alongside some real illustrations by frankstephenson design.

All three vehicles REO intends to release are detailed and pictured here. The T4X is the work truck; the T4C is the crew cab pickup; and the S4C is a family SUV. All three ride on the same steel ladder frame, and are even identical in every way from the B-pillar forward. It’s beyond the B-pillar where each, naturally, differ based on their specific use cases.

The T4X will be the first to go on sale (targeting late 2028) according to the brand, and it has a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed. Said bed measures 79.1 inches long and 70.6 inches wide. The tailgate has some neat features with integrated cup holders, recesses for phones or tablets, and bottle openers on either side.

In a recent development, the T4C crew cab trades some of the bed length for passenger space, as it seats up to five people. That remarked, the bed is still fairly long, at 54.1 inches in length.

Meanwhile, the S4C seats six, and notably has a shorter rear overhang than the trucks to help with the departure angle for off-roading. The cargo area can be accessed via a side-hinged tailgate, and the rear glass even drops down into the door.

Industry observers note that these are the unique body style features REO is detailing for now, but they all have much more in common than they do differences. For example, each REO vehicle will be equipped with a naturally aspirated four-cylinder engine that the manufacturer indicates is designed for longevity, drive-ability and towing more than outright performance. A six-speed manual transmission comes standard, while a six-speed automatic gearbox will be optional. Every REO is also fitted with part-time four-wheel drive, allowing you to select 2WD or 4WD High/Low via a floor-mounted lever. A locking rear differential will be optional for those who want it.

Expect a bumpy ride, because in addition to the body-on-frame construction, all REOs will have solid axles front and rear. Disc brakes will be fitted up front, but drums are used in the back. You’ll steer with hydraulic assistance, and 17-inch steel wheels will be wrapped by all-season tires. Should off-roading be in your future, a “Ransom Package” will be optional, adding off-road tires with unique off-road wheels, upgraded dampers/leaf springs, and a 2.5-inch suspension lift. (You’ll also get orange accents that designate it as the Ransom Package model.).

Photos of the interior aren’t available, but REO says physical controls will “take prominence.” Unlike the Slate Truck, power windows come standard, but the seats are manually adjustable. There will still be screens, though, as REO says it comes with a digital cluster and display for navigation and media.

As of now, the T4X is slated to start at $21,500 and be sold in a direct-sales model (no dealers). The T4C is meant to starts at $25,000, and the S4C at $28,500. The organization states it aims to assemble all three in Texas. While the T4X is meant to reach buyers in late 2028, neither the crew cab pickup nor the SUV have predicted on-sale dates yet; if you want one, REO is taking refundable $25 deposits.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination. A deal could be unveiled as soon as December, which would make it the largest merger ever, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.

In a recent development, according to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved. December is the target, but early 2027 is also on the table.

One of the variables on the table is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. So, as expected, this is shaping up as SpaceX absorbing Tesla, not the other way around.

Recent findings suggest that that fits the valuations. SpaceX is worth over $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, while Tesla sits around $1.5 trillion. For scale, the record for a single deal has long been Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000, and even SpaceX’s roughly $250 billion purchase of xAI (a private manufacturer at the time) earlier this year would be dwarfed.

According to recent reports, neither organization commented. Tesla stock rose as much as 1.9% on the report.

Industry observers note that we’ve been tracking this since May, when Musk first floated merging the two companies weeks before the SpaceX IPO. At the time, we called it the fourth time Musk would make a more than $1 billion self-dealing transaction, after SolarCity, Twitter/X, and Tesla’s $2 billion xAI investment that turned into SpaceX stock.

Industry observers note that then, in October, Tesla’s proxy filing read like a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has sat on SpaceX’s board since February. The ballot for the December 3 meeting is limited to re-electing Musk, chair Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to terms through 2029, plus a say-on-pay vote and the auditor.

A day later, Musk confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.

The governance piece is where Tesla shareholders should pay the most attention.

According to recent reports, musk owns about 20% of Tesla but controlled roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares, according to its S-1. Swapping Tesla shares for SpaceX shares means trading one-share-one-vote for a organization where Musk’s control is effectively locked in.

And the deal itself pays Musk. Under the change-in-control terms in his 2025 CEO award, the operational milestones drop out and the market cap test runs at the deal price, with earned shares vesting immediately. Based on the share count in the proxy, a deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion (about a 33% premium to where it trades now) would clear the first market cap tranche on the spot. His 286 million restricted shares from the 2018 package also accelerate on a change in control.

Bloomberg reports that one of the main obstacles is how to ring-fence Tesla’s China business. A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s defense and government work and Tesla’s China footprint as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.

That’s the same issue behind the Wall Street Journal’s July report that Tesla was weighing a sale or spinoff of its China operations, which Musk denied. Giga Shanghai is Tesla’s most productive factory and builds more than half of its cars. It shipped 67,829 vehicles in October alone.

In a recent development, politics is the other wild card. Congress flipped to Democrats in the midterms, and they’ve noted Musk’s companies and his political ties will get a hard look. Bloomberg previously reported the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

I suspected that the midterms might accelerate the timeline. The Dems don’t take office until January, and Musk likely wants to move this as far along as possible before then.

Recent findings suggest that no rational independent board would offer $1.5 trillion (much less $2 trillion) for Tesla. It is a shrinking EV organization with a few fantasy projects that are not delivering. But endlessly diluting other stockholders is his thing.

According to recent reports, as for the “independent committees”, those are obviously a joke. No one believes that, but it’s not like Tesla’s shareholders would care at this point. Tesla’s stock has been a dud for 4 years, and shareholders’ best chance to see a return is another self-deal with Musk.

Tesla is a car and energy company with falling car sales, and it would get folded into a rocket, satellite, and AI company that’s valued at a premium to it and controlled by one person.

It has been revealed that this is the end game. At least, it looks like Elon is running out of companies to fold together to hide underperformance.

Sources indicate that if you’re following Tesla because of its energy business, the cheapest way to tap into that transition at home is still putting solar on your own roof. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage. Tech Report: The Man With No Butt
