Smartwatch blood pressure monitoring was okay. AI is making it better.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease.
  • In a recent development, while that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced.
  • That context is worth keeping in mind when considering new research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the United States Food and Drug Administration cleared the Apple Watch’s Hypertension Notification Feature last year, some saw it as a turning point in the fight against one of the leading causes of cardiac disease. Rather than booking a doctor’s appointment and strapping a bulging cuff around one’s arm, people could instead receive passive hypertension alerts from the watch’s optical sensors to track blood flow patterns. Watch wearers who were previously unaware that they had signs of this ever-common “silent killer” would receive an alert advising them to seek out a clinician. Early intervention could mean a better chance at beginning life-saving interventions.

In a recent development, while that sounds great, the reality of smartwatch hypertension tools is more nuanced. Apple’s own validation data highlighted that their feature would miss around 59 percent of people with undiagnosed high blood pressure. Newer United States population level research from the University of Utah and the University of Pennsylvania went a step further, and warned that the absence of an alert could give wearers a false sense of security, potentially making them less likely to go get a proper cuff screening. The feature, in other words, isn’t necessarily harmful, but it also isn’t a medical silver bullet.

That context is worth keeping in mind when considering new research from scientists at Google and a clinical partner from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recently published in the journal Nature. The team claims they created a new AI system that pairs with a consumer smartwatch to passively detect signs of high blood pressure, “with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed blood pressure devices.”.

The newly introduced system draws on two sensors already found in many consumer smartwatches: an optical pulse sensor (which tracks changes in blood volume at the wrist) and an accelerometer. An AI algorithm then analyzes several days of  readings, factors in the wearer’s height, and then calculates the probability that they have hypertension.

Google’s system builds on Apple’s approach by adding in the watch’s accelerometer to the mix, which can pick up the faint wrist vibrations of each heartbeat. The results look promising. In initial screenings, the combined system caught more cases of high blood pressure than a standard office cuff reading, though it still missed about a third of cases. And while the researchers involved still advise against using the tool as a substitute for seeing a doctor, it’s potentially another step forward in attempts to use common wearable tech to catch underlying signs of disease earlier.

“By gently prompting at-risk individuals to step into a clinic for formal assessment, this technology holds the potential to significantly close the global awareness gap and catch hypertension before it causes permanent cardiovascular damage,” Google researchers note in a blog post.

Sources indicate that heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the U.S. , claiming more than  900,000 lives in 2023 alone. Chronic high blood pressure (referred to as hypertension medically) is one of the key early risk factors. Around half of all Americans likely have it, but an estimated four in ten people don’t know they have it, partly because it often does not present with any clear symptoms. And while hypertension is treatable when caught early, many simply don’t see a doctor often enough to be screened regularly. That combination of an invisible condition and spotty screening makes the problem an attractive target for always-on smartwatch sensors.

Sources indicate that the sensors on commercial smartwatches can pick up useful data, but those signals still need to be interpreted by an AI model. In this case, Google says it trained its system on nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data collected from 2,109 people. The optical sensor captures the shapes of each pulse wave at the wrist, while the accelerometer shows signs of the subtle physical vibrations that occur at the wrist when blood is ejected from the heart into the aorta. Both of those signal data are cut into 5-second PPG and ACC waveforms. The AI converts those signal snippets into numerical summaries, which Google refers to as an “embedding.”.

Over time, the AI model was able to pore over those different numerical values and determine which types of pulses are likely associated with hypertension. By analyzing data collected from one wearer to the next, the AI sees numerical patterns that distinguish one person’s signals from another. But simply relying on a measurement from one point in time risks introducing what the researcher calls “environmental noise” that can skew results. To account for all that noise, they aggregated the sensors’ data over multiple days of use to establish a wearer’s persistent state. That data then gets fed into a logistic regression classifier, which comes out with a score corresponding to a person’s likelihood of having hypertension.

In a recent development, the team tested their system on 196 participants over seven days of real-world monitoring, checking their results against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, which they refer to as the “gold standard” in the field. The AI smartwatch system ultimately detected hypertension with a sensitivity of 65.8 percent. That means 65.8 percent of people who were proven to have hypertension were accurately identified by their AI system. That’s far from perfect, but it was still higher than the 55.3 percent caught by initial office cuff readings in the study.

“Taken together, the results show that our system can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed BP devices in the existing clinical framework,” Google notes.

Like Apple before it, Google and the other medical researchers involved in this story were quick to stress that these findings, noteworthy as they may sound, shouldn’t lead people to think of this system as a complete replacement for clinical blood pressure monitoring .Going to see actual human doctors isn’t going away anytime soon, but this system, if widely accessible, could help nudge more people towards getting checked out.

#52643. Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1786 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

Cycling Taught Me How to Suffer—a Lesson That Helped Me Lose 140 Pounds and Find Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles.
  • According to recent reports, I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more.
  • According to recent reports, IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that SEPTEMBER 2026, THE week of the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal and the city was lousy with bicycles. On most corners, a upcoming pack of amateur cyclists gathered. Bixi—Montreal’s bike share program—was represented, but as a garnish to the inundation of mountain, beach, fixie, and road bikes, along with their riders from around the world, taking over the city. I watched all this in awe. Cycling changed me because it taught me how to suffer. The sport familiarized me with the type of suffering that wrecks you, but you put yourself through it on purpose. You suffer to emerge resilient and better.

According to recent reports, I'd heard elite cyclists—guys like Toms Skujins, Sean Quinn, and Mike Woods—talk about this pain in passing, but I was in Montreal to learn more. I wanted to know if they saw the power of suffering in the same way I did.

According to recent reports, IN 2001, I was an obese drug addict. Checking into rehab that year put a number to my weight: 536 pounds. I’d been diagnosed with congestive heart failure, drugs were rapidly killing me, and I was motivated to change. Once I’d been sober for a year, I was able to see that my weight was causing me suffering.

Standing was a herculean effort, placing my feet in the right spot to support me, calculating the angle my knees would be in at the apex of my shifting mass, deep breath, locked core, and a hope and a prayer that I didn’t topple. Tying my shoes was done in bursts of held breath and near-blackouts. I slept sitting up, because the pressure of my chest caused me to choke and gasp. I could once soothe that suffering with food and drugs and kick that discomfort down the road a bit, but in sobriety I needed healthy outlets.

According to recent reports, I’d successfully managed lose 100 pounds before my wife tricked me into going to the gym. When she’d ask that I go, I’d tell her that the gym was a place for fit people. So she bought me a package with a personal trainer, noted I could flake on the appointments, but I’d be flushing money down the toilet if I did. I went, but I was geared towards avoidance, and whenever something in the gym got hard, I’d just tell the trainer I couldn’t do it.

Riding a bike was something I did during outings with my wife and little kids maybe a few times a year. We’d cram our minivan full of bikes, find the flattest part of the Venice bike path, and slowly cruise for ten minutes at a time. Getting them back into the car was the hardest thing I had to work through.

Little did I know that someday cycling would be the key to changing my life.

It has been revealed that ROUND AND ROUND I went losing and regaining weight. In 2009, after getting down to 300 pounds and ballooning back up to over 400, faced with having to start over once again, I turned my sights to running.

I tried running on a desolate stretch of the LA river near my house in Studio City. Not only was I unbearably slow, running hurt. My flat feet sent electric jolts of white-hot pain cascading up and through my body. That first day, I’d wrapped my ankles so tightly with ace bandages that my toes went numb. My feet were no better off and my nipples bled. The next day I could barely stand. The suffering didn’t stop when I stopped running. My feet, ankles, knees, and hips hurt long after—and I had no control over it.

In a recent development, with running out, but I turned to an old beach cruiser in our shed. The street we lived on was relatively flat, but every street branching off it was a steep climb. After a few rounds on my street, I decided to be ballsy and see how long I could last going uphill.

It has been revealed that my legs were screaming, but there was no electric jolt of pain in my pedal stroke. My heart thundered, my mind told me I had to stop. But without the jarring jolt I got when my feet hit the ground while running, I knew I could go further.

Despite never riding my bike uphill as a kid, despite weighing 400 pounds, despite every physical and mental signal in me telling me to quit, I made it up to the top of that hill, up to Mulholland and Laurel Canyon, and it was glorious. Fighting through that urge to stop was incredible; getting to the top even more so. The pain while running was a warning that stayed with me after I stopped. The pain of cycling uphill was legs, lungs, and heart. I could push through it, and it stopped when I stopped.

It has been revealed that I asked Tour de France cyclist Mike Woods about this distinction of suffering when I was in Montreal. “Suffering is a bit of a misnomer for endurance events. Are you really suffering? It’s elected, you know?” he told me. “You choose the pain, you choose when to stop, you choose when to keep going. I don’t truly suffer. Suffering is when you don’t choose for that pain to be inflicted on you”.

And then he mentioned something that really resonated with me: “But it does prepare you for real suffering, when you have something bad happen to you in life. Doing endurance events, I find—it’s fake suffering, but when you have those bad moments in your life, you’re better prepared to manage them.”.

According to recent reports, AFTER THAT HILL climb, I started riding my bike regularly, eventually graduated to a mountain bike, and then to a road bike. I rode to the top of every mountain in Los Angeles. I discovered I was capable of so much more than my mind or body allowed me to believe. Legs screaming, heart pounding, mind numbing, this was suffering, and I found that I loved it. And, like Woods stated, I found that the more I suffered on a bicycle, the less I suffered off it.

“One day at a time, one pedal stroke at a time. Just move forward,” Toms Skujins, a two-time Latvian road race champion, told me in Montreal. “When you’re racing, you can stop at any point. You’re the one doing the damage, you know? That’s very voluntary suffering, because there’s, obviously, things in the world that happen where you don’t choose to suffer, and you have no choice there. Here… if your legs are screaming too much, you can just stop. For me, that kind of suffering is definitely easier to take.”.

Within my first year of cycling, I was riding every day. There was a loop that took me from Studio City over the hill to West Hollywood. I’d cross Los Angeles, ride up PCH, cross the Santa Monica Mountains, and ride back to Studio City along Ventura Boulevard. It got me 100 miles and 8,000 feet of climbing, and I did it a few times a week. I’d do shorter 30- to 50-mile rides on the remaining days.

Industry observers note that sean Quinn, a US pro cyclist, gets it: “It sounds easy when you’re sitting on the couch, but when you’re actually in that moment suffering, your body’s basically sending you all the signals it can to make you just do anything else, just stop, stop the suffering,” he told me. “There’s no instant fix to a lot of your suffering. You have to be patient, accept that it’s gonna be shitty for a while, and wait it out, and keep a cool head, and eventually it does get better. Of course, you have to take action.”.

It has been revealed that when I was riding every day, I got down to 213 pounds. I’d like to say I stayed there. But I went back to work, stopped riding, my diet unraveled, and over the next few years, I gained nearly all of it back.

In 2016, 400 pounds again, I ruptured the biceps tendon in my right arm and had to have surgery to repair it. As a sober guy, I turned down the post-op painkillers. I was up all night in pain and had to work the following day. On set, with the motion of production buzzing around me, the pain was dull, but it was unrelenting, just like a ride up Angeles Crest Highway, more than 120 miles out-and-back, with over 13,000 feet of elevation gain. I hadn’t chosen the injury, but I had chosen to go without the pills, and that reminded me of the pain on the bike, something I picked and something I knew would come to an end. I’d remind myself of that and go back to learning my lines and preparing for the scene.

In a recent development, that day reminded me that I knew how to do this. So I got back on a diet, and by 2018 I was down to 260, and I’ve held steady there ever since.

Riding a bike taught me that I could suffer now in benefit of tomorrow. It’s been the most powerful lesson I’ve learned about myself.

ON THE DAY of the elite men’s road race, we fans lined the streets. There was dedicated bike parking near the finish line—Fans Village Bonjour Montreal—with thousands of bikes in neat rows. We all lined up to watch the attacks, riders going solo for that long and treacherous circuit. An American, Brandon McNulty, went off the front with about three laps to go and won the World Championship this year. It was thrilling to see. At the press conference afterward he said, “I was just dying, but I kept pushing.”.

In a recent development, leaving Canada, I couldn’t help but think that I shared something with everyone else there for the races. A secret membership, dues paid in sweat, and a code, to respect and revel in my voluntary suffering.

I’d gone to Montreal to ask the riders if they saw suffering the way I did, and in different words, all three told me that what you do on the bike carries over into the rest of your life. I’d thought cycling taught me how to suffer, but what it did was give me a place where I was in control of it, where I could make it a practice, so that when the suffering of life came along, the suffering I had no control over, I was better equipped to deal with it.

Recent findings suggest that if your domicile happens to exist, say, under a large boulder, you might not have heard that Grand Theft Auto VI is finally arriving at the stroke of midnight on November 19. Those of us who watch television, browse the web, scroll social media, listen to the radio, read the newspaper, flip through magazines, or consume outside info in any way are well aware of the video game, however. It’s the latest installment of the immensely popular “Grand Theft Auto” series, which combines a (surprisingly deep) vein of car culture with an immersive open world full of theft, fighting, drugs, and other violent delights.

It has been revealed that while the previous games came out on a semi-regular schedule of one every few years, it’s been 13 trips ‘round the sun since the last one hit stores. (GTA VI’s development has been so delayed, it even inspired a meme.) Suffice it to say, there’s a lot of pent-up anticipation—even enough to spark half-founded panic headlines about millions of people around the world call in sick to play. But there’s another report that puts a bit more solid of a figure on the excitement around the game. According to digital analysis firm SensorTower, GTA VI has already racked up $1.65 billion in pre-sales ahead of its launch.

That correlates to a little over 17 million orders for the game so far, according to the report, with 75 percent of pre-sales going for the PlayStation 5 version and the other 25 percent for Xbox Series X|S consoles. The chart shows a fairly typical exponential curve growth over the last five months since pre-sales kicked off: a long period of incremental gains, followed by rapid acceleration in the last few weeks.

And GTA VI-based revenue seems likely to keep coming in to creator Rockstar Games’s coffers at quite a clip, considering initial reviews for the game have been stellar so far. While it may not be your typical automotive-themed driving game, the latest release seems all but sure to guarantee Grand Theft Auto remains a serious part of car culture for some time to come.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.
  • Recent findings suggest that these expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date.
  • According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

Recent findings suggest that these expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep challenges, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

It has been revealed that “This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”.

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these complications.

In a recent development, according to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

It has been revealed that A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:.

Research indicates that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

Sources indicate that “This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” noted Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”.

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are right now two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

Industry observers note that there are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:.

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

Sources indicate that “Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” noted Pier.

These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

  • Industry observers note that I was transfixed by the ritual of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

Industry observers note that I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two complications at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” says Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

According to recent reports, meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

As skincare and scent merges into a brand-upcoming category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” claims Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

In a recent development, skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” indicates Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

Sources indicate that it’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

It has been revealed that but it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do says.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”.

In a recent development, dr. Queller indicates that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”.

Deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she indicates the skin barrier may already be impaired.

It has been revealed that so, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she notes it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

The latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, says Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence crucial cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study demonstrated that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

It has been revealed that it’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The newly introduced Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

It has been revealed that future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume.

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-latest blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist.

Recent findings suggest that salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

Sources indicate that A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum.

Sources indicate that each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

So, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”.

Recent findings suggest that what is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this upcoming fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”.

SD: Yes. You got it. Your brain is doing fine.

SD: And to make matters even more confusing, though, Holtz points out the biggest scientific problem of all: Gonzo’s nose isn’t actually a beak at all.

SD: In birds and turtles, the beak is the mouth. It’s the actual jaw bone covered in hard keratin. But for Gonzo, that big purple nose thing is an extension sitting above and in front of his mouth. It doesn’t have the hard shine of keratin, and it doesn’t move like an elephant’s trunk. Holtz claims it’s an anatomical structure that is basically unheard of in vertebrate biology.

In a recent development, AC: Leave it to Gonzo to have a face that literally defies anatomy. My whatever theory still holds water.

According to recent reports, SD: It really does. And Darren Naish actually had a great philosophical take on this. He pointed out that nobody asks what creature other Muppets like Animal or Elmo are because they don’t have distinct anatomical clues. But Gonzo has just enough real anatomy, feathers, a beak, three fingers, a chicken for a partner, to make our human brains desperate to categorize him. As Naish put it, “Specificity invites scrutiny.”.

AC: And the more details you give us, the more obsessed we become with solving the puzzle.

SD: Exactly. So whether he’s an ibis, a dinosaur, or an evolutionary wild card, science still can’t give us a tidy one-word label.

Recent findings suggest that AC: Which means, Sarah, there is only one logical thing left for us to do. We’ve heard what the paleontologists and the developmental biologists have to say, but what does the man behind the Muppet think?

Industry observers note that SD: That’s right. Up next, Annie sits down with the one and only David Goelz, the legendary puppeteer who has performed and voiced Gonzo since day one. She asks Dave what he thinks Gonzo really is, how that iconic character was born, and whether he agrees with Team Dinosaur.

AC: Truly a dream come true. That’s right after this quick break.

Welcome back. I am thrilled to welcome Muppet legend Dave Goelz. Dave has been the voice and spirit, I’d say, of Gonzo for 50 years. He also originated a number of other beloved characters, including Uncle Traveling Matt of Fraggle Rock fame, as well as Muppets Zoot, Beauregard, and of course, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew.

Dave, thank you so much for being here.

Dave Goelz: Well, thank you for having me.

AC: Yes. So we have spent this episode trying to figure out what Gonzo might be in a scientific sense, and since you know him better than anyone, what do you think Gonzo actually is?

DG: Well, I can answer from our particular corner of the field.

In a recent development, when the Muppets started out, they tended to be almost always abstract characters. There was one humanoid in their first series. The series was called Sam and Friends, and Sam looked like a, a person, but everybody else on the show looked like things we’d never seen before. And then when we went on Sesame Street, this is before, before I was there, actually, they went on Sesame Street, they, it stayed with abstract characters, Ernie and Bert, Grover.

Grover is considered a monster. And they stayed with those abstract characters for quite a long time, and then when we did The Muppet Show, all of a sudden we were surprised to see pigs and chickens….

DG: I remember thinking, “This is weird, the Muppets are abstract. Why do we, why do we have a pig?” You know? “Why do, why do we have a chicken?” It was just an interesting transition ’cause that’s when we went more literal with, with species. Getting around to answering your question, I don’t know what Gonzo is. I have no idea. He was something that Jim built for a previous special, as you know, and when it came time to do The Muppet Show, Jim asked me to do this character who was kind of a loser outsider who does stupid acts and thinks they’re high art.

According to recent reports, and then he asked for them to pull Gonzo out. Or that, that puppet that wasn’t Gonzo yet.

DG: And so that was what I started with.

AC: What were your first impressions when you saw the puppet itself?

DG: Well, I had seen it before, so it wasn’t a surprise, but it was this pathetic-looking little guy, who had very downcast eyes. He was sort of limited, but I just started making a character out of him, and what my interest in him has always been is his character. And iin that one character, I found that it mirrored me. The reason that it did was because Jerry Juhl, who was our head writer and a very wise person and very funny and mischievous person, could see, I guess, that I was new.

Sources indicate that I had no business in show business. I had no training. I had no acting training. We just started The Muppet Show, and Jim tossed me in, and I felt very out of place. I just go, “I don’t belong here. What am I doing in this room?” And so Jerry Juhl helped write Gonzo to be appropriate to where I was in life, and that was phase one. He was an outsider. He had a little bit of a baby talk accent….

DG: like a true newbie. And then as time went by, and I’m talking about years, I got more confident, and then one of our writers, Bill Prady, he started writing Gonzo as being very upbeat and enthusiastic. Like, “That is so cool,” you know, and, and just up for anything, and that became phase two of his character, which coincided with me being more comfortable in my new world And then phase three came when Jerry Juhl wanted to include Dickensian prose in the Muppet Christmas Carol film.

It has been revealed that he needed that narrative prose in there, but didn’t want to have a narrator, and he had the idea, because we were very close friends, and he’d watched me go through therapy, and he’d watched me deepen and soften and evolve. He had the idea of letting Gonzo speak those lines.

AC: I feel like people have been asking this question since we all met Gonzo. Why do you think people care so much?

Sources indicate that DG: Oh, I think I’ve learned a lot about that in the last, I don’t know, 10 years, let’s say. Whenever I appear at a museum or introduce a screening, people come up to me, and so many people come up and say, “Thank you. Gonzo gave me permission to be different.”.

According to recent reports, DG: He legitimized it. He made it cool. And a lot of these people are on the spectrum, and they are lovely people who have a hard time in life. And it was unintentional on my part. I didn’t know that they were, that Gonzo was having this effect on people, but he did.

It has been revealed that and then about four months ago, I, I realized suddenly that, oh, wait a minute, no, no, this was unconscious on my part. I knew I was different. I didn’t belong in show business. I should be on my parents’ couch, you know, watching on the other end.

AC: Yeah, I feel like, I’m sure people have noted this to you, you know, I think people think of Kermit as the heart of the Muppets, and they think of Gonzo as kind of the soul of the Muppets, and I think that nebulousness around what he is, of like not really knowing, I think it allows a lot of people, you know, myself included, that you can find a piece of yourself in him.

If you’ve ever felt excluded or weird, because he is not defined, there is lots of room to sort of hold a piece of him as a fan.

According to recent reports, DG: Oh, Annie, that’s absolutely true. Absolutely true. He’s been that for people, and I have to say also that the Muppets as a whole are like that, too. They function the same way.

DG: Jim was a lover of characters. He hired characters. He hired all sorts of unusual people and found something for them to do and let them shine. It’s like I didn’t create Gonzo. It was me and the writers and Jim and the workshop. And these qualities exist in every single character, and there’s somebody out there who responds to every single one.

AC: You have a little bit of like an engineering and design background, right?

Industry observers note that DG: I do, yeah. I was an industrial designer by training.

AC: Yeah, and I think especially lately there’s this sort of stark line between art and science, but you know, what we see, especially at Popular Science, is we see really amazing innovations can happen when art and science overlap.

So how do you bring a little bit of that engineering mind to playing a Muppet?

Industry observers note that DG: A couple of things. First of all, when I first began, I already knew how to build puppets because I was trained as a designer at Art Center College of Design, and the design process was something that my dad inculcated into me, and then ArtCenter set in place.

It has been revealed that and the design process that I use is about defining the problem, whether it’s a character, a performance, a glasses case, a typewriter. Whatever it is, it’s very key to know what the problem is, and it’s not always obvious. Listen, the reason I love that approach is that the more you hone in on the problem, the clearer the solution becomes.

It has been revealed that AC: One final question. Because we’re Popular Science, I must ask about the Muppets’ preeminent scientist, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew-.

In a recent development, AC: whom, of course, you also perform. If Bunsen, or Dr. Honeydew, he earned his degree, won a Nobel Prize, what do you think it would be for?

DG: Well, first of all, the idea is preposterous-.

In a recent development, DG: On its face. That’s a great question. If he won a Noble Prize, what would it be for? A Nobel Peace Prize. All he’s done in life is make stupid inventions and hurt his assistant.

In a recent development, DG: So it really is a preposterous notion. I can’t even answer it.

I can’t. It’s just a mind-boggling question. I don’t have any idea how he could possibly be recognized for anything. I will tell you this, that Bunsen was, Bunsen was derived from a lot of scientists that I knew when I was in Silicon Valley. It wasn’t anybody directly, but it was this whole idea of being focused on electrons and being focused on tiny, tiny, very specific things, and losing the big picture.

It has been revealed that DG: Yeah. ‘Cause it’s interesting you know, a scientist might be way deep into making a laser interferometer, and the science of it would be so riveting. And then my job was to come along and say, “Okay, what does it look like? How do you use it?” So I was, like, the user end of this whole deal. And, and so as a generalist, I could view the science world and the engineering world, and, uh, poke a little fun at it.

Industry observers note that AC: Absolutely. Science is fun. We like to remind people.

AC: I will take off my journalist hat just for a second and say thank you so much for doing the podcast, but also just thank you so much for Gonzo. What you noted about people who have maybe been called different or weird, it definitely resonates with me.

I’ve loved the Muppets my entire life, and being called weird my whole life is such a compliment because there’s so much joy and whimsy in the weirdos of Muppets, and Gonzo is such the epitome of that, that I thank you so much, Dave, for joining us today.

According to recent reports, DG: Been my pleasure. Thanks, Annie.

SD: Oh my gosh, was your inner Muppet heart exploding while talking to Dave? Yes. He seemed so wonderful.

According to recent reports, AC: Yeah, he is just an absolute gem of a human. I did not even try to keep my fandom in check ’cause he’s a legend, and he’s genuinely meant so much to me as a Muppet fan.

SD: He’s the best. Oh my God. So after hearing from Dave and all of our biologists where do you, Muppet expert, officially land on the taxonomy of a Gonzo?

According to recent reports, AC: Okay, I started the episode firmly on team whatever, but now I kinda love the idea that Camilla is casually dating a prehistoric dinosaur. But I also like the idea that Gonzo doesn’t have to be defined. He can be something different for everyone, like, whatever they need him to be.

SD: But the dinosaur theory does make his cannonball catching stunt seem a lot more on brand for a T-Rex relative.

And if you like our show, leave a rating and a review.

AC: Thank you, team. Thank you, Dave, and thanks all you Muppets for listening.
